newsitem.title: FINLAND: OPSTOCK CUTS FINNISH BOURSE FIRMS' PROFIT FORECAST.
newsitem.headline: OPSTOCK CUTS FINNISH BOURSE FIRMS' PROFIT FORECAST.

text.p: Finnish brokerage Opstock said in a statement on Thursday it had lowered its forecast for Finnish listed companies' combined 1996 net profit to 18.3 billion markka from 20.3 billion.
Last year, the combined net profit was 22.6 billion markka.
Cooperative controlled OKOBANK's Opstock also lowered its profit forecast for 1997, to 23.3 billion markka from 25 billion.
The revisions followed recent profit warnings, Opstock said.
"Despite the fall in profits, Opstock expects dividends paid to rise this year compared to 1995," it said, forecasting 1996 divididends at 6.86 billion markka and 1997 dividends at 7.33 billion.
Opstock saw little scope for shares to rise in the near term but said that low interest rates gave scope for Finnish shares to narrrow the valuation gap to Europe in two to three years.
The Helsinki bourse market capitalisation equals about nine times forecast 1997 earnings while the average corresponding P/E ratio on European bourses is 15, Opstock said.
"We will narrow that gap, maybe to some 12," Opstock chief analyst Jaakko Niemela said told a news conference.
"The upward potential for shares in the next 12 months is about 11 to 13 percent," Opstosk said in its statement.

Niemela said that while financial markets have revalued Finnish debt this year -- bringing interest rates clearly lower on hopes that Finland would join Economic and Monetary Union -- next year the turn would come for equity revaluation.

"Our view is that the Finnish valuation is closing in on the European, therefore, as currency risk is removed, returns in the next two to three years should be above (Finnish and European) long-term average," Niemela said.
He also said that a linkage of the Finnish markka to the Exchange Rate Mechanism was priced in the financial markets and that there was litlle scope for even lower interest rates.
"A link would have little impact anymore," he said.
